analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top tax rate on individuals' long-term investment gains from 28% to 21%.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have excluded a quarter of investment gains from tax and capped the top rate on them at 21 percent, died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. Dennis DeConcini's bill would have let individuals, estates, and trusts deduct 25 percent of their net capital gains from taxable income, and would have capped the tax on investment gains at 21 percent instead of the 28 percent top rate set by the 1986 Tax Reform Act. Under the 1986 reform, capital gains were taxed the same as wages; this bill would have moved gains back toward special, lower treatment. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that realize capital gains — profits from selling stock, real estate, or a business. The savings are proportional to the size of the gain, so the largest benefits would go to the people with the largest portfolios, who are overwhelmingly high-income; a small saver would get a small break and no one without taxable gains would get anything.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors with capital gains, mostly high earners

how_it_helps.text: Allows a deduction equal to 25 percent of net capital gains for individuals, estates, and trusts, removing a quarter of investment gains from taxable income.
Caps the tax on net capital gains at 21 percent, down from the 28 percent top rate in effect after the 1986 Tax Reform Act taxed gains like ordinary income.
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 1988, so it would have lowered tax bills for the year the bill was pending, not just future years.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar of the cut is revenue lost, which means larger deficits or higher taxes on other income to make it up; because the benefits concentrate at the top, the burden of financing them would spread to everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury and all other taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The deduction and rate cap carry no income limit, and realized capital gains flow disproportionately to high-income households, so most of the tax savings would have gone to the wealthiest investors rather than to ordinary savers.

The bill would have reduced federal revenue every year it stayed in effect — larger deficits or offsetting taxes on other income — unwinding part of the base-broadening bargain of the 1986 reform, which had just ended the old capital gains exclusion in exchange for lower rates on work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Anyone who sells an appreciated asset would pay less tax, and supporters argue lower rates encourage investment and reduce the 'lock-in' that keeps people from selling. But the savings scale with the size of the gain, so the money concentrates at the top while the lost revenue is shared by everyone through deficits or other taxes. Congress had weighed this same trade-off in 1986 and chosen to tax gains like wages; this bill would have quietly reversed that choice without paying for it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action until the 101st Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Dennis DeConcini introduced the bill on May 1, 1989, to restore the capital gains deduction and cut the top rate on gains to 21 percent.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Finance Committee never acted on the bill, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue that a 21 percent capital gains cap would have surrendered, and taxpayers were spared the larger deficits or offsetting taxes. Investors with large gains never received the cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; large investors lost the cut

for.name: Sen. Dennis DeConcini
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore a 25 percent capital gains deduction and cap the top rate on gains at 21 percent; no colleagues joined him.

against.name: Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so there is no measurable partisan split — just one Democrat acting alone, with both parties invested in the 28 percent rate after the 1986 reform.

industries.note: The bill sets no income limit, and capital gains concentrate at the top, so the 21 percent cap and 25 percent deduction would have delivered the largest tax savings to the wealthiest investors — paid for through higher deficits or taxes on other income.

industries.industry: Financial services (brokerages, asset managers, private equity)
industries.note: Lower taxes on gains encourage more selling and investing, which increases fee and management income for the financial industry. The benefit is a side effect of the tax cut rather than a direct transfer, but the industry's interest ran with the bill's.
